openingMessage: Failure is not fatal, but failure to change might be.
openingWhy: A near-miss is the well telling you exactly how it plans to hurt somebody — free of charge. The crews that end up in the report are rarely the ones who got no warning. They're the ones who turned the warning into a story instead of a change.
leadershipThought: Your awareness has to be higher than your intent. Intent doesn't matter if the impact is wrong. Operate in a diverse environment — different backgrounds, different beliefs, different life experiences.

specialFocus.title: Five Miles From the Shop: Fog, Dark and a Driver Who Wouldn't Wait
specialFocus.why:
Jacob, start here. Wednesday morning, on Highway 176 north of Midland, less than five miles from the shop, in fog and dark, a driver was weaving in and out between two semis. That driver tried to pass the second semi with no way to see what was coming and almost hit Ralph Forbes head-on. Ralph took the ditch to avoid it. The trailer jackknifed, pushed the truck back out into the oncoming lane, and the semi hit it.

Thank God, the semi driver turned toward the ditch at the very last second. Instead of a T-bone, it was a sideswipe at an angle, and that probably saved Ralph's and Jimmy Cooper's lives. The other driver caused this. Ralph and Jimmy were doing their job and driving to work.

Ralph and Jimmy are both okay and home with their families.

The hit came at an angle, not a T-bone
Highway 176, Wednesday morning: fog and dark, five miles from the shop
“We're in the same fight together. We all want the best for our families and ourselves.”
— Mike Lyons
🌫 FOG AND DARK: five for the drive
  • Slow down to what you can see. If you can't stop inside the distance you can see, you're too fast. Low beams in fog, never brights.
  • Back off the semis. Double your following distance in fog and dark. Six seconds or more.
  • Let the weaver go. Somebody driving crazy around you? Ease off, give them the road, and keep your eyes on your way out.
  • Never pass what you can't see past. On a two-lane in fog, there's no pass worth it.
  • Too thick? Get off the road and wait it out. Pull well clear, hazards on, and call your lead. Late is better than never.
✓ WHERE WE SAW IT THIS WEEK: say these names
  • Justin Pack, Hughes #1: five days running with nothing to fix.
  • The week so far: Medlin and Popillion's stop over a leaking casing, Jobe's tag and cones, Zarate's eight sites, Bailey and Marquez-Salazar's trailers, Easley and Flores on supervision, Fontenot, Blassingame, Haugh and McKenzie. That's the same fight, every day.

specialFocus.standardLabel: Week 23: Operational Discipline Starts Behind the Wheel
standard: Speed for the conditions, not the sign. Fog and dark cut the speed limit for you.
Low beams in fog, lights on all day, and keep the glass clean.
Six seconds or more behind any semi in fog or dark.
Let the weaver go. Don't race, don't block, don't speed up. Back off and give them the road.
Know your way out. Shoulder, ditch, open lane: always know where you'd go.
Seatbelts, every seat, every trip. Phone down, and nobody drives tired.

scenarios.title: The Weaver in Your Mirror
scenarios.body: It's 5:30 in the morning on a two-lane, the fog is thick, and you're behind a semi. Headlights come up fast behind you, swing out, duck back in, swing out again. That driver wants by and can't see any better than you can. What do you do? Ease off. Open a gap so they have somewhere to go. Don't speed up and don't hold your ground. Watch the oncoming lane for them, and know where your shoulder is. Jacob, ask the circle: on your drive this morning, where was your way out?

questions: What does too fast for the fog look like on your route?
When somebody's driving crazy around you, what's your first move?
Thanksgiving is one week from today. Who's checking that you got home, and who are you checking on?
